_comment: How the C# army behaves, recorded by ArmyReferenceTests.MeasureTheArmy.
Flat world, seam at z=0, no trade flow, no truck: everything that moves
here is the army's own doing. Seeded 20260901, sampled every five seconds
for ninety.
Four passes, because the top-level one cannot be compared to the core on
its own. The army REPLACES its dead - Army.Reinforce, one tank a side
every six seconds and faster the further behind it is - so `n` in the rows
is an establishment being held up, not a count of survivors. Over ninety
seconds it loses 125 tanks and lands 115 replacements to stay at ~40 of
48. Read `lost` and `arrived` in the density series before reading `n`.
The shape to reproduce, read off these rows:
- both sides enter at |z| ~ 77.5, tightly grouped (spread ~0.9)
- armour closes at about 6.8 m/s, infantry at about 2.6
- they are in contact by t=15 and the first armour losses are at t=10-15
- from t=30 it is a steady grind: armour |z| ~ 25 with a spread near 20,
infantry |z| ~ 15-20, both sides holding roughly 70 of 72 infantry
- neither side breaks through: the means oscillate, they do not cross
passes.attrition and passes.core-size are the SAME army with replacement
switched off - what the core was held to for firing and death, before it
had reinforcement. passes.core-size-reinforce is the establishment AND the
replacement the core actually fields, and is the one its army is accepted
against now.

tolerance._comment: metres on the mean, and units on the count

_comment: Enemies inside the 46 m gun range per living tank, how far the armour is
spread along x, how many tanks have a target at all, how many died, and
how many replacements walked on. Same run as the rows above.
The earlier reading of these numbers - "the C# army keeps 71-83% of its
armour, so the core must be too lethal per shot" - was wrong, and the
lost/arrived columns are why: the C# army does not keep its armour, it
buys new armour. 125 lost, 115 arrived, 90 seconds. Per-shot lethality
in the core already matches C# exactly (reload 1.4-3.2 s, 0.55 to
connect, damage 11-24 against 60-99 hit points, which is C# 1.1-2.4
against 6-10 at the ten-fold scale).
The series now runs the full ninety seconds. It stopped at t=35 before,
which is why the core could be reported as "shooters fall to zero by
t=60" against a reference that had nothing to say at t=60.
The first two have reinforcement off (ReinforceSeconds pushed past the
run). Two arrivals still get through, because the first tick of a deficit
fires before the cadence is reset - one per side. Everything after that
is attrition and nothing else. The third has it on.
attrition: the recording establishment, 24 armour and 72 infantry a side.
core-size: 12 and 36 a side, which is what the core fields - UNITS is 96
and every fourth index is a tank - so a comparison against this one is
not also a comparison of two differently sized armies.
Both collapse the way the core does: one side is ground down, the
survivors end up with nothing inside the 46 m gun, and the shooting stops
for good. That is the answer to whether the core fires and dies like C#.
It does. What it does not have is Army.Reinforce.
The core's establishment WITH replacement, and the only pass its own
reinforcement is to be accepted against. Steady state from t=15: 19-22
tanks of 24 alive, 59 lost and 55 arrived over ninety seconds, and
between 12 and 17 tanks with a target at every single sample - the
shooter count never reaches zero, which is the failure replacement
exists to prevent.

xBands is the armour's |x| in the bands the core is measured in, added because xSpread is a standard deviation and cannot tell a peak with stragglers from a flat spread. Counters that read Armour and draw nothing: every field that existed before was recorded again and came back identical.
